summary:
Zambian law criminalises consensual same-sex conduct and the prohibition is enforced. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law falls within the conduct the law reaches. Amnesty International's campaign account of 26 November 2024, 'Madalitso's story', describes a 36-year-old medical professional who by November 2024 had served three years of a sentence imposed for consensual same-sex acts; his imprisonment removed a trained clinician from a health system already short of staff.

Police are a documented source of risk rather than protection. The US State Department's 2021 country report records police perpetrating violence and verbal and physical harassment on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation, and prolonged detentions of LGBTQI+ people. Advocacy groups reported that police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTI individuals, with fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha, roughly $30 to $900. The 2022 report adds that when police detain LGBTQI+ people they often threaten charges under other laws to extort payment for release, and it found no credible reports that government agents condoned violence.

Prosecutions for same-sex conduct have relied on forced anal examinations. Human Rights Watch's July 2016 report 'Dignity Debased' documents the practice in Zambia, where prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal examinations as court evidence in sodomy cases, including a mass trial of about twenty men. Victims describe the examinations as painful, degrading sexual violence; Amnesty International in 2014 called them tantamount to torture and scientifically invalid, and the World Health Organization and medical authorities have condemned them.

The government rejects recognition and protection of LGBTQI+ rights. The 2021 State Department report found the government continued to reject such recognition and protection, and the 2022 report found no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ people. President Hakainde Hichilema's statement of 30 May, recorded in the 2022 report, opposed basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage and was followed by a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults.

Freedom of expression and assembly on LGBTQI+ matters is effectively barred. The government does not permit advocacy of LGBTQ rights, and the 2021 State Department report concluded that freedom of expression or peaceful assembly on LGBTQI+ matters remained nonexistent. In 1998 Vice President Christon Tembo called for the arrest of people promoting gay rights, and the Registrar of Societies stated he would refuse to register any LGBTQ organisation. In The People v. Paul Kasonkomona (2013), an activist arrested after calling for decriminalisation on a television talk show was cleared: the Magistrate Court and then the High Court held he was reasonably exercising his right to freedom of expression, and the High Court rejected the soliciting, public place and immoral purposes charges. The government contested that decision.

Societal violence against LGBTQI+ people is frequent and often communal, with little recourse from police: threats, stalking, vandalism and hate crimes including murders are documented. The 2021 report found LGBTQI+ people at risk of societal violence arising from prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of the law. In May 2014 residents of Marapodi in Lusaka apprehended two suspected lesbians and demanded their arrest, and in January 2015 an openly gay man was attacked by a mob that reportedly included three police officers. Most LGBTQI+ people in Zambia are closeted because of the risk of targeting, and lesbians are especially vulnerable within the country's patriarchal structure.

Discrimination in employment, housing, education and health continued through both reporting years. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination in health care, but limited standards exist: the Health Professions Council of Zambia's 2014 Code of Ethics bars practitioners from discriminating in patient management on the basis of sexuality, and the Ministry of Health's 2022 Zambia Consolidated HIV Guidelines require facilities to serve all adolescents regardless of sexual orientation or sexual behaviour. The 2021 State Department report records LGBTQI+ people facing an inability to access healthcare services.

Social attitudes are mostly negative, shaped by evangelical religious influence and colonial-era attitudes and by perceptions that homosexuality is immoral or a form of insanity. A 2010 survey found 2 percent of Zambians considered homosexuality morally acceptable. Anti-LGBTQI+ mobilisation is organised: the NGO Zambia Against People with Abnormal Sexual Acts (ZAPASA) was formed in 1999 to combat homosexuality.
tangentialFactors:
The 2010 survey figure of 2 percent sits nine points below the 11 percent recorded in Uganda in the same survey.

Human Rights Watch's 2016 report covers at least eight countries. It records forced anal examinations as less frequent in Zambia than in Egypt or Tunisia, while Zambian prosecutors have used medical reports from such examinations as evidence in sodomy cases.
localsOnly:
Section 158(3) of the penal code, amended in 2005, provides that a child who commits gross indecency with another child of the same sex, in public or private, or who attempts to procure such acts, is liable to such community service or counselling as the court may determine in the best interests of the child. There is no parallel offence for minors of the opposite sex.

The National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Policy of 2015 recognises sexual orientation and gender identities as central aspects of being human.

As of July 2007 no public or private programmes provided HIV-related counselling to men who have sex with men. Adult HIV prevalence was about 17 percent, and the government's National AIDS Control Program does not address same-sex relationships. Societal discrimination in access to health care and in access to education is documented.

Attitudes among younger Zambians are shifting slightly toward greater openness, credited to internet access and rapid digitisation exposing people to more stories from different parts of life. In 2013 Christine Kaseba, wife of then-President Michael Sata, said silence around men who have sex with men should end and that no one should be discriminated against on the basis of sexual orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No information in the source inventory addresses trans-specific healthcare or medication in Zambia.

Gender-marker and identity-document rules for trans travellers, and any entry or visa screening that could expose a traveller's status, are not sourced.

Access to sex-segregated facilities such as toilets and changing rooms is not addressed by any source.

The outcome of the government's challenge to the 2013 Kasonkomona acquittal is not recorded.

HIV service data date from July 2007 and the attitude survey from 2010; no more recent figures are available here.
